chunks.text: Bamboos are a large group of mostly evergreen, perennial flowering plants making up the subfamily Bambusoideae within the grass family Poaceae, comprising over 1,460 known species across roughly 115 genera, split into tropical woody bamboos (Bambuseae), temperate woody bamboos (Arundinarieae) and herbaceous bamboos (Olyreae); the largest, Dendrocalamus sinicus, can produce culms around 46 m tall and 36 cm across, making it the largest member of the entire grass family. Structurally, bamboo culms are hollow between the nodes and, lacking the secondary (cambium-driven) wood growth of true trees, emerge from the ground already at their full diameter and simply mature over three to five years rather than thickening with age — yet the resulting material still achieves a strength-to-weight ratio competitive with timber, with tensile strength for some species (e.g. Bambusa tulda) reported up to roughly 400 MPa under test conditions. Bamboo is also among the very fastest-growing plants on Earth, with some species documented growing up to about 910 mm (nearly a metre) in a single 24-hour period under ideal conditions, and typical growing-season rates in temperate species of 30-100 mm a day; this rapid biomass accumulation, combined with tolerance for marginal and degraded land, is why bamboo is increasingly discussed as a candidate for afforestation and carbon-sequestration projects, with some estimates (carrying real uncertainty and flagged for further citation in the source) suggesting bamboo stands can store on the order of 100-400 tonnes of carbon per hectare. Ecologically it anchors entire food webs — bamboo makes up roughly 99% of the giant panda's diet, and it is similarly essential to red pandas in Nepal and bamboo lemurs in Madagascar, while mountain gorillas and elephants eat parts of it too — though fast-spreading 'running' (rhizomatous) species can also become locally invasive, shading out native vegetation and altering soil chemistry, in contrast to slower-spreading clumping species. Economically and culturally, bamboo is deeply woven into daily life across Asia: it is used for scaffolding on construction sites, for traditional housing (nipa huts in the Philippines), for suspension bridges (one Chinese example on record from 960 CE), for furniture, fishing rods, paper pulp (China, Myanmar, Thailand and India are the major pulp producers), woven crafts, musical instruments and classical painting traditions in China and Japan, and extensively as food — bamboo shoots are eaten across the continent, though raw shoots contain taxiphyllin, a compound that can release cyanide, so they must be boiled or steamed (commonly for 20 minutes or more, with water changes) before eating. In India specifically, fermented bamboo shoots are a recognised regional delicacy under different names — khorisa in Assam, kardi (used in the soup amil) around Sambalpur in Odisha, and kirla sukke in Konkani cuisine — while the seeds of naturally dying plants are eaten in southern India as 'bamboo rice'; bamboo also feeds India's domestic paper industry (for example mills at Chandrapur in Maharashtra) and underpins traditional reed pens (kalam/boru), and Sikkim has promoted bamboo-based water bottles as a plastic-reduction initiative. Perhaps bamboo's single most dramatic and least-understood biological trait is gregarious (mass) flowering: many species flower only at very long, species-characteristic intervals — commonly cited examples run to 65 or 120 years — with every plant in a genetically related cohort flowering together across huge distances (including cloned/propagated individuals grown far from their origin), after which the flowering plants typically die; the longest documented interval, around 120 years, belongs to Phyllostachys bambusoides, and the underlying biological trigger remains scientifically unresolved, commonly described only loosely as an internal 'clock' that eventually redirects the plant's energy from vegetative growth into one final, synchronised reproductive event.

chunks.source: Mongabay-India — bamboo gregarious flowering in Chandaka-Dampara Wildlife Sanctuary, Odisha (2018)
chunks.text: This report documents a real, recent Indian instance of gregarious bamboo flowering: in December 2017, Indian thorny bamboo (Bambusa bambos) flowered simultaneously across several square kilometres of the Chandaka-Dampara Wildlife Sanctuary near Bhubaneswar, Odisha, triggering local concern over a possible rodent population boom and consequent crop damage in surrounding farmland — a well-known secondary effect of mass bamboo flowering, since the sudden, enormous pulse of nutrient-rich bamboo seed can temporarily boost rodent breeding success and survival. Importantly, the article quotes experts cautioning that a rodent/crop-damage outbreak is not an automatic or guaranteed consequence of every gregarious flowering event — local ecological conditions, the surrounding mix of forest and farmland, and existing rodent populations all affect whether a bloom actually cascades into a famine-like event, and ongoing monitoring rather than assumed catastrophe is the recommended response. This more measured, case-specific framing is a useful complement to the much more dramatic and historically documented 'Mautam' cycle in India's northeast, discussed separately below, since it shows that gregarious flowering's ecological and social consequences vary considerably by region and species rather than being uniformly catastrophic.

chunks.source: India Environment Portal — "Mautak will flower" (Mizoram bamboo-famine cycle)
chunks.text: This piece covers the most famous and historically consequential bamboo-flowering event associated with India: the roughly 48-50 year cycle of gregarious flowering in Melocanna baccifera (locally mautak), concentrated in Mizoram and neighbouring northeastern states, known as 'Mautam' (literally close to 'bamboo death'). When mautak flowers and sets seed en masse, the resulting glut of seed drives a sharp, well-documented rise in jungle rat populations (rodent fertility is reported to increase on this seed-rich diet), and the resulting rodent swarms then move into and devastate standing food crops once the bamboo seed is exhausted, historically producing severe regional famine. The most catastrophic recorded episode followed the 1959-60 flowering, which according to the source contributed to roughly 3,000 deaths from the ensuing famine and helped fuel an armed insurgency in the region — unrest that was a direct contributing factor to the eventual creation of Mizoram as a separate state. The source is honest that the precise biological trigger and timing mechanism behind gregarious bamboo flowering is still not fully explained by science, and notes that accounts differ somewhat on the exact date of the most recent flowering cycle (sources elsewhere point to around 2006-2007), underscoring that even this well-studied cycle still carries real scientific uncertainty.
